specAnchors.text: describe the formation of carbon dioxide from the thermal decomposition of metal carbonates, including copper(II) carbonate

primer.text: From Composition of Air you already know that carbon dioxide is one of the small components of air and the gas that limewater can identify. This note shows a second way the gas appears: heating metal carbonates until they break apart, leaving a metal oxide behind and releasing carbon dioxide, with copper(II) carbonate as the required example.

modules.title: What is thermal decomposition?
modules.opening: Thermal decomposition describes reactions in which a substance breaks down because of the action of heat. One important family belongs to the metal carbonates: for metals in the lower half of the series, heating breaks their carbonates apart. The breakdown leaves the metal oxide behind and gives off carbon dioxide gas.
keyPoints: Thermal decomposition is the breaking down of a substance due to the action of heat.
Carbonates of the less reactive metals, those low in the series, break apart on heating.
The general pattern is metal carbonate giving metal oxide plus carbon dioxide.
The carbon dioxide released escapes as a gas, which is what makes the breakdown visible.
Copper(II) carbonate is the example of this breakdown named by the specification.

low.restatement: Heat alone can split a substance into simpler pieces, and that is what thermal decomposition means. Heat a metal carbonate from the lower half of the reactivity series and it splits into a metal oxide and carbon dioxide gas.
low.analogy: Like a parcel that springs open when the temperature rises: the contents separate into two clearly different items, a solid and a gas.
low.examPointer: Learn the general word pattern metal carbonate giving metal oxide plus carbon dioxide; it writes half the answer for you.

medium.restatement: Thermal decomposition is driven by heat alone, with no other reactant present, and the metal carbonates of the less reactive half of the series undergo it readily on heating. Each carbonate splits into the corresponding metal oxide while carbon dioxide escapes as a gas, which is the change to describe in full.
medium.analogy: Picture a two-layer sandwich held together by a glue that melts when warmed: the layers fall apart cleanly, one staying on the plate and one drifting away as vapour.
medium.examPointer: State that heat is the only cause, name both products, and link the carbonate's position in the reactivity series to how readily it breaks down.

modules.title: Thermal decomposition of copper(II) carbonate
modules.opening: Copper(II) carbonate is a green powder that breaks down readily on heating. As it decomposes, the solid slowly darkens because black copper(II) oxide is being produced, while carbon dioxide escapes. Passing the gas through limewater confirms it: the limewater turns milky, which is the standard test for carbon dioxide.
keyPoints: Copper(II) carbonate is a green powder that decomposes readily on heating.
The green solid darkens little by little as black copper(II) oxide forms.
The gas given off can be tested by passing it through limewater, which turns milky.
The symbol equation is CuCO3 (s) → CuO (s) + CO2 (g).
In words: copper(II) carbonate gives copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide.

low.restatement: Heat the green powder and it darkens to black as copper(II) oxide forms, with carbon dioxide bubbling off. Bubble that gas through limewater and the milky turn confirms what it is.
low.analogy: Like a leaf changing colour as it dries out: the colour shift is the visible signature of the substance becoming something new.
low.examPointer: The colour story green to black plus the milky limewater is a classic observation question; know both ends of it.

medium.restatement: On heating, copper(II) carbonate splits readily into black copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide gas, matching the equation CuCO3 gives CuO plus CO2. The colour change from green to black marks the new solid, and the milky turn of limewater identifies the escaped gas as carbon dioxide.
medium.analogy: Think of a two-clue detective test: the solid's new colour names the oxide, and the limewater's milky turn names the gas.
medium.examPointer: Write the equation with state symbols when asked, and link the milky limewater to carbon dioxide by name, not just by colour.

glossary.definition: The breaking down of a substance into simpler substances due to the action of heat alone.
A compound of a metal with carbon and oxygen, which many of them give up carbon dioxide on heating.
A clear solution that turns milky when carbon dioxide is passed through it, the standard test for the gas.
The ordered list of metals arranged by how readily they react, which also predicts how their carbonates behave.
The solid compound of a metal with oxygen, left behind when a metal carbonate decomposes.
